answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1934–1996 · Astronomer, planetary scientist & science communicator, Cornell University
answer.sourceLine: Sagan wrote it himself, in his own chapter — chapter 11, “The Age of Exploration” — of Carl Sagan’s Universe (Cambridge University Press, 1997), the volume of papers from the October 1994 Cornell symposium held for his sixtieth birthday. One letter separates the printed sentence from the version that circulates: Sagan wrote “the courage of our questions and the depth of our answers,” singular; the plural “depths” is the wording in the White House transcript of President Obama’s Rutgers commencement address of 15 May 2016.

trail: Full-text search of the Internet Archive scan puts the sentence in the 1997 Cambridge volume: “…courage of our questions and the depth of our answers, our willingness to embrace what is true…” in Carl Sagan’s Universe ↗.

The chapter is Sagan’s own, not another contributor quoting him — the book’s contents page reads “11 The Age of Exploration CARL SAGAN 141” ↗, and the preface describes “a chapter by Carl on ‘The Age of Exploration.’”

The volume itself: Carl Sagan’s Universe, ed. Terzian & Bilson, Cambridge University Press, 1997 ↗ — papers from the October 1994 Cornell symposium for Sagan’s sixtieth birthday. The Internet Archive holds the scan ↗.

Wikiquote still lists the line as misattributed ↗, on the grounds that nothing predates Obama’s 2016 Rutgers speech. The 1997 book, and a printed “—Carl Sagan” credit in Lewis Pinault’s Consulting Demons (January 2000) ↗, both come earlier.

author.name: Carl Sagan
author.heading: Who was Carl Sagan?
author.bio: Carl Sagan (born 9 November 1934, died 20 December 1996) was the David Duncan Professor of Astronomy and Space Sciences at Cornell University, where he also directed the Laboratory for Planetary Studies. He is best known for co-writing and presenting the 1980 PBS series Cosmos: A Personal Voyage, which reached audiences in dozens of countries, and for a shelf of bestselling books that made him one of the most influential science communicators of his generation. The sentence on this page comes from the last stretch of his career — a chapter written for the book that grew out of his own sixtieth-birthday symposium at Cornell.

misattribution.heading: The wording, and the people it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This one is genuinely Sagan — which makes it unusual for a quote that circulates entirely without a source. What has gone wrong is the wording, and the paper trail.

items.why: Sagan’s printed sentence is singular: “the depth of our answers.” The plural appears in the White House transcript of President Obama’s Rutgers commencement address of 15 May 2016 ↗, and a full-text search of digitized books turns up no book at all using “the depths of our answers, our willingness” ↗.

Compilations in the Pocket Book of Mindfulness series print the first half of the line under the Italian writer’s name — the scanned text reads “Cesare Pavese: We can judge our progress by the courage of our questions…” ↗, immediately after a genuine Pavese line about remembering moments rather than days. Nothing connects the sentence to Pavese beyond that page.

Wikiquote files the line as misattributed ↗, crediting it to a 2014 self-published book and stating that no reference to it exists before Obama’s 2016 speech. It is in a 1997 Cambridge University Press book ↗, and Lewis Pinault’s Consulting Demons, published January 2000 ↗, already prints it signed “—Carl Sagan.”

The two get swapped constantly. Wikiquote sources “If we long for our planet to be important, there is something we can do about it. We make our world significant by the courage of our questions and by the depth of our answers” to Cosmos (1980), p. 193 ↗. That is a different sentence from a different book, and it has no “what feels good” clause.

misattribution.truthLine: Sagan really wrote it — in “The Age of Exploration,” his own chapter in Carl Sagan’s Universe (Cambridge University Press, 1997) ↗ — but with “depth,” singular.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: In October 1994 Cornell threw a two-day symposium for Carl Sagan’s sixtieth birthday. The papers became a book, Carl Sagan’s Universe, published by Cambridge University Press in 1997 — and Sagan contributed a chapter of his own, “The Age of Exploration.” The famous sentence sits inside a passage about where human significance actually comes from: not from being cosmically special, and not from the honesty of our politicians, but from what we are brave enough to ask and honest enough to accept in reply.

It is a sharpened version of a thought he had used before. Cosmos (1980) has the gentler formulation — “We make our world significant by the courage of our questions and by the depth of our answers” — and the two lines are constantly swapped for each other online. The later version adds the clause that gives it its edge: our willingness to embrace what is true rather than what feels good.
context.detailsSummary: A note on why this looks like a fake (and isn’t)
detailsBody: The quote has every marker of an internet fabrication: no source anywhere on the big aggregator sites, a famous name attached, and a tidily inspirational shape. Wikiquote currently files it under Misattributed, with an editor’s note claiming it originated with a 2014 self-published book and that no trace of it exists online before Obama’s May 2016 Rutgers speech.

Both halves of that note are wrong. The sentence is printed in a 1997 Cambridge University Press book, in a chapter by Sagan himself; and it was already being quoted, with Sagan’s name attached, in Lewis Pinault’s Consulting Demons, published in January 2000.
